knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle -6, -2, 3\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle -4, 1, 2\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle -22, 2, 11\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-6s-4t &=-22 \\ -2s+t &=2 \\ 3s+2t &=11\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-6 & -4 & -22 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 11\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2 \leftarrow R_2-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)R_1$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-6 & -4 & -22 \\ 0 & \frac{7}{3} & \frac{28}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row is $0=0$, so it adds no restriction. Back substitute in the two nonzero rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{\frac{28}{3}}{\frac{7}{3}}=4 \\ s&=\frac{-22-(-4)(4)}{-6}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Verify every coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)(-6)+(4)(-4)&=-22=-22 \\ (1)(-2)+(4)(1)&=2=2 \\ (1)(3)+(4)(2)&=11=11\end{aligned}
$$

All three coordinates agree, so the vector lies on the plane. Therefore,

$$
s\cdot t=(1)\cdot(4)=4.
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: The pair $s=1,t=4$ satisfies all three coordinates; the vector lies on the plane.
Correct. The common pair satisfies all three equations and gives $s\cdot t=4$.

knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle 1, -2, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle -3, 6, 2\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 7, -14, -8\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-3t &=7 \\ -2s+6t &=-14 \\ s+2t &=-8\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & 7 \\ -2 & 6 & -14 \\ 1 & 2 & -8\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2 \leftarrow R_2-(-2)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-(1)R_1$, then $R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & 7 \\ 0 & 5 & -15 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row is $0=0$, so it adds no restriction. Back substitute in the two nonzero rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{-15}{5}=-3 \\ s&=\frac{7-(-3)(-3)}{1}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Verify every coordinate:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)(1)+(-3)(-3)&=7=7 \\ (-2)(-2)+(-3)(6)&=-14=-14 \\ (-2)(1)+(-3)(2)&=-8=-8\end{aligned}
$$

All three coordinates agree, so the vector lies on the plane. Therefore,

$$
s\cdot t=(-2)\cdot(-3)=6.
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: This is $t$ alone; the question asks for $s\cdot t$.
The pair $s=-2,t=-3$ satisfies all three coordinates; the vector lies on the plane.
Correct. The common pair satisfies all three equations and gives $s\cdot t=6$.

knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies on a Plane

question.:question/problem:
Determine whether $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, where $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}&=\langle 2, -1, 1\rangle \\ \mathbf{c}&=\langle -2, 1, -2\rangle \\ \mathbf{u}&=\langle 12, -7, 10\rangle\end{aligned}
$$

If it does, select the value of $s\cdot t$ in $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$. Otherwise, select the statement that $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in\Pi$ exactly when the same values of $s$ and $t$ satisfy all three coordinate equations. Expanding the vector equation gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2s-2t &=12 \\ -s+t &=-7 \\ s-2t &=10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -2 & 12 \\ -1 & 1 & -7 \\ 1 & -2 & 10\end{array}\right]
$$

Apply $R_2 \leftarrow R_2-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)R_1$, then $R_3 \leftarrow R_3-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)R_1$, then $R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & -2 & 12 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{array}\right]
$$

The last row gives $0=-1$, a contradiction. No pair satisfies all three equations. Thus $\mathbf{u}$ does not lie on $\Pi$. A product obtained from only two coordinates is not a valid answer.
